**185. Responsibilities of Professor In-Charge – Consultancy**

**185.1. Role Overview**

• The Professor In-Charge acts as the operational coordinator and single point of contact for all consultancy-related activities within the division/department.

• They ensure proper planning, execution, monitoring, and documentation of consultancy projects in alignment with institutional expectations.

**185.2. Key Responsibilities**

**i. Assessment of Faculty Skill Sets**

• Identify and maintain a record of:

> o Specialized knowledge domains
>
> o Technical competencies
>
> o Certifications or training relevant to consultancy

• Match faculty capabilities with suitable consultancy opportunities.

**ii. Infrastructure Mapping**

• Document and periodically update:

> o Available lab equipment and tools
>
> o Software resources
>
> o Support staff availability

• Evaluate readiness of the division to undertake specific types of consultancy projects.

**iii. Consultancy Records Management**

• Maintain accurate records of:

> o Project proposals and approvals
>
> o MoUs and client correspondence
>
> o Budget and financial tracking
>
> o Deliverables and reports submitted

• Ensure data is readily available for audits, reviews, and future references.

**iv. Progress Review & Corrective Action**

• Participate in joint review meetings with the Dean (Consultancy) and HoD.

• Monitor:

> o Milestone achievement
>
> o Client feedback
>
> o Resource utilization

• Take corrective actions where deviations or delays are identified.

• Submit progress updates to higher authorities as required.

**186. Guidelines for Undertaking Consultancy Services**

**186.1. Scope of Consultancy Work**

• Faculty or the University can undertake consultancy in the following forms:

> o Testing and Validation
>
> o Design and Fabrication
>
> o Software/Hardware Development
>
> o Prototyping and Simulation
>
> o Theoretical or Computational Analysis
>
> o Knowledge-based Advisory
>
> o System Design and Implementation

• Consultancy can be offered on a chargeable or non-chargeable basis.

• University infrastructure and resources may be used for execution.

**186.2. General Guidelines**

**i. Eligibility and Approvals**

• All faculty members are encouraged to take up consultancy assignments.

• Prior approval from the Vice Chancellor (VC) is mandatory.

**ii. Academic Responsibilities First**

• Consultancy assignments must not interfere with:

> o Scheduled classes
>
> o Lab sessions
>
> o Other official academic duties

**iii. Budgeting for Resources**

• Any requirement for consumables, special tools, or equipment must be:

> o Clearly itemized in the budget
>
> o Procured from the consultancy charges only

**iv. Expense Coverage**

• All expenses related to:

> o Travel and transportation
>
> o Site visits and field work
>
> o Report preparation and printing

• Must be covered from the consultancy budget.

**v. Use of Institutional Infrastructure**

• University facilities such as:

> o Laboratories
>
> o Office space
>
> o Water, electricity, and internet

• May be utilized with prior intimation.

**vi. Completion Certification**

• A certificate of successful completion must be obtained from the client/consulting organization.

**vii. Funding Protocol**

• All payments should be made by the client in the name of the University (not individual faculty).

**viii. Proposal Preparation**

• Consultancy proposals must include a comprehensive budget covering:

> o Consultancy fee
>
> o Consumables and equipment
>
> o Travel and field expenses
>
> o Documentation and incidentals

**186.3. Distribution of Consultancy Charges**

*Norms for revenue sharing and fund allocation to be outlined here (not provided in this excerpt).*

• Typically includes:

> o Share to the faculty/team
>
> o Share to department/division
>
> o Administrative overhead to the University

• Should follow university-approved financial guidelines.

**187. Marketing Consultancy Services**

**187.1. Division-Level Brochure Development**

• Each academic division must prepare a brochure that showcases its consultancy potential.

• The brochure must include:

> o Faculty Profiles

• Name, designation, specialization

• Past consultancy/project experience

> o Laboratory & Infrastructure Details

• Key equipment, software, and testing facilities

> o Service Offerings

• Areas of consultancy: design, prototyping, testing, development, advisory, etc.

• Sample projects or case studies

> o Contact Information

• Professor In-Charge, HoD, Dean (Consultancy)

• The brochure should be:

> o Professionally designed and periodically updated
>
> o Available in print and digital format (PDF/HTML)

**187.2. Industry Outreach and Circulation**

• The University shall appoint a dedicated marketing officer to:

> o Identify and build a database of potential industry clients
>
> o Circulate the division-wise consultancy brochures to:

• Local industries and SMEs

• Corporate R&D units

• Government and public sector agencies

> o Schedule meetings, webinars, or visits to promote offerings

**187.3. Minimum Engagement Requirement**

• Every division is expected to undertake at least one consultancy project per academic year.

• Divisions should:

> o Actively follow up on leads generated through brochure marketing
>
> o Convert academic projects or faculty expertise into practical consulting engagements
>
> o Collaborate with Dean (Consultancy) to align outreach efforts with institutional goals

**188. Planning, Monitoring and Control of Consultancy Services**

**188.1. Planning of Consultancy Services**

• Dean (R&D) is primarily responsible for:

> o Developing an Annual Consultancy Plan based on:

• The capability reports submitted by departments/HoDs

• Service requirement analysis from industries and external agencies

> o Collaborating with Heads of Departments (HoDs) to:

• Identify the readiness and strengths of each division

• Align potential consultancy projects with faculty expertise

**188.2. Inclusion into University Planning**

• The consultancy plan prepared by the Dean (Consultancy) is:

> o Submitted to the University Development Council (UDC)
>
> o Integrated into the overall institutional development plan along with academic, research, and extension activities

**188.3. Procurement and Reporting**

• Consultancy procurement involves:

> o Engaging with industries based on brochure distribution, direct marketing, and faculty references
>
> o Converting identified opportunities into formal consultancy contracts

• Quarterly Reporting to VC:

> o A progress report on consultancy procurement efforts must be submitted to the Vice Chancellor once every three months
>
> o This includes:

• No. of consultancy leads pursued

• Proposals submitted

• Projects secured

**188.4. Assignment of Consultancy Services**

• Once a consultancy contract is secured:

> o It is assigned to the relevant division based on:

• Faculty skill set

• Laboratory and infrastructure availability

• Timeline and resource demands of the consultancy

> o The HoD and Professor In-Charge are informed and responsible for execution

**188.5. Monthly Review and Control**

• Progress of all active consultancy services is:

> o Reviewed monthly by the Dean (R&D) in consultation with the HoD and faculty in charge
>
> o Tracked for:

• Milestone completion

• Resource utilization

• Client communication

• Financial tracking

• Monthly Progress Report is submitted to the Vice Chancellor highlighting:

> o Ongoing consultancy work
>
> o Status updates and deliverables
>
> o Issues and corrective actions taken

**189. Research-Based Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

Research-Based Consultancy involves leveraging the research expertise, facilities, and analytical capabilities of academic institutions to solve real-world problems or develop new solutions for external clients, such as industries, government agencies, or non-profits. It is a focused type of consultancy where the outputs are rooted in systematic investigation and evidence-based analysis.

**189.1. Key Characteristics of Research-Based Consultancy**

| **Aspect**         | **Details**                                                                   |
|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Focus              | Application of academic research to address practical or theoretical problems |
| Clients            | Industry, government departments, research councils, NGOs, start-ups          |
| Output             | Research reports, feasibility studies, testing results, models, white papers  |
| Expertise Involved | Faculty, research scholars, labs, and centers of excellence                   |
| Duration           | Can range from a few weeks to several months or years                         |

**189.2. Objectives of Research-Based Consultancy**

• Transfer academic knowledge to address real-world challenges

• Build long-term collaboration between academia and industry

• Generate funding for further institutional research

• Support policy-making and product development

• Enhance institutional visibility and impact

**189.3. Examples of Research-Based Consultancy**

| **Discipline**        | **Example Consultancy Work**                                     |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Civil Engineering     | Structural health monitoring for bridges                         |
| Computer Science      | AI model development for predictive maintenance in manufacturing |
| Environmental Science | Water quality and environmental impact assessment reports        |
| Management Studies    | Market research and consumer behavior analysis                   |
| Biotechnology         | Testing and validation of biomedical products                    |
| Agriculture           | Soil nutrient studies and precision farming recommendations      |

**189.4. Process of Research-Based Consultancy**

1\. **Problem Identification**

> o Client approaches the institution with a specific problem or need.

2\. **Proposal Preparation**

> o Faculty prepares a detailed proposal outlining scope, methodology, timeline, and cost.

3\. **Approval and Agreement**

> o MoU or contract is signed between the institution and client.

4\. **Execution**

> o Research is conducted, often involving lab work, data collection, modeling, and analysis.

5\. **Reporting**

> o Final deliverables, such as research findings and recommendations, are submitted.

6\. **Closure and Feedback**

> o Project closure with feedback from the client; revenue distribution follows.

**189.5. Deliverables May Include**

• Technical Reports

• Feasibility Studies

• Data Analysis Reports

• Design and Prototype Models

• Proof of Concept Studies

• Policy Recommendations

**189.6. Confidentiality and Intellectual Property (IP)**

• NDAs (Non-Disclosure Agreements) may be signed to protect client data.

• Institutions must clarify IP ownership in the consultancy agreement:

> o IP may remain with the client, institution, or be jointly held, depending on terms.

• Patent filings or publications resulting from the work should respect the agreed IP clause.

**189.7. Revenue and Benefit to Institution**

• Revenue generated supports:

> o Faculty incentives
>
> o Research infrastructure
>
> o Student research involvement

• Enhances NAAC/NBA accreditation scores under Research & Development criteria.

**189.8. Support Structures Required**

• R&D Cell or Dean (R&D) for project oversight and policy adherence

• Legal team for agreements and IP handling

• Finance department for billing and fund management

• Dedicated laboratories and research centers

**189.9. Best Practices**

• Maintain transparency and documentation at all stages

• Involve postgraduate and research students to build capacity

• Share outcomes in annual reports and accreditations

• Align consultancy with institutional research strengths and priorities

**190. Educational Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

Educational Consultancy refers to the advisory and support services provided by Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) to other academic bodies, government agencies, private institutions, and educational startups. The goal is to enhance educational practices, quality, governance, curriculum development, training, and institutional development using the academic and administrative expertise of HEIs.

It leverages the HEI's knowledge base, faculty expertise, infrastructure, and experience to offer tailored educational solutions and build institutional capacity.

**190.1. Scope of Educational Consultancy**

Educational consultancy in HEIs can be broad and multidisciplinary. The scope typically includes:

| **Domain**                               | **Explanation**                                                                                                               |
|------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Curriculum Development                   | Helping other institutions design, revise, or align curricula with regulatory bodies (e.g., AICTE, NEP 2020, UGC guidelines). |
| Faculty Training & FDPs                  | Conducting Faculty Development Programs (FDPs) to upgrade teaching skills, technology integration, and pedagogy.              |
| Outcome-Based Education (OBE) Assessment | Assisting institutions in setting up CO-PO-PSO mappings, rubrics, attainment levels, and assessment methods.                  |
| Accreditation                            | Guiding institutions through NAAC/NBA/ISO accreditation and audits, including preparation of Self Study Reports (SSR).        |
| Governance & Strategy                    | Advising on institutional planning, academic administration, internal quality assurance systems (IQAC), and benchmarking.     |
| Educational Technology                   | Recommending and implementing Learning Management Systems (LMS), ERP, online platforms, or digital classroom tools.           |
| Policy Advisory                          | Drafting education-related policy documents, quality manuals, or institutional vision-mission statements.                     |

**190.2. Objectives of Educational Consultancy**

1\. **Improve Educational Quality:** Provide solutions to improve academic standards, teaching quality, and student outcomes.

2\. **Share Expertise:** Use HEI's faculty knowledge and research to support other institutions or systems.

3\. **Enable Accreditation and Compliance:** Help other institutions meet the requirements of quality assurance bodies (NAAC/NBA).

4\. **Promote National Educational Goals:** Align practices with NEP 2020, SDGs, and outcome-based education (OBE).

5\. **Foster Collaboration:** Build academic networks, partnerships, and visibility across institutions.

**190.3. Process of Educational Consultancy in HEIs**

Here is a step-by-step process for how educational consultancy typically works:

| **Step**                   | **Explanation**                                                                                               |
|----------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1\. Need Identification    | The client institution approaches the HEI with a specific need (e.g., NAAC preparation, curriculum redesign). |
| 2\. Proposal Preparation   | The HEI prepares a proposal outlining objectives, deliverables, timeline, cost, and involved faculty/experts. |
| 3\. MoU/Agreement Signing  | A formal agreement is signed between both institutions, detailing IP rights, confidentiality, and payments.   |
| 4\. Project Execution      | The HEI delivers the consultancy work – conducting workshops, curriculum reviews, training sessions, etc.     |
| 5\. Review & Feedback      | Feedback is collected from the client institution; modifications or follow-ups may be recommended.            |
| 6\. Final Report & Closure | A completion report is submitted along with certification of services rendered.                               |

**190.4. Examples of Educational Consultancy**

| **Field**             | **Example**                                                                                                      |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Engineering Education | A university department helps a rural engineering college align its B.Tech curriculum with AICTE model syllabus. |
| Accreditation         | Experts from a NAAC A++ college guide a private college to prepare documentation for its first NAAC cycle.       |
| Faculty Development   | A central university conducts a 5-day online FDP on “Digital Pedagogy and Bloom’s Taxonomy.”                     |
| Governance            | An HEI helps a newly formed autonomous college in setting up its IQAC, Academic Council, and Board of Studies.   |

**190.5. Benefits to the HEI (Consultancy Provider)**

1\. **Revenue Generation –** Fee-based consultancy can support institutional funding.

2\. **Faculty Development –** Engaging in consultancy enriches faculty with real-world exposure.

3\. **Reputation and Branding –** Enhances the profile of the HEI as a center of academic excellence.

4\. **Collaborative Opportunities –** Opens pathways for MoUs, research collaborations, and student exchange.

5\. **Support to National Goals –** Contributes to the growth of the educational ecosystem as envisioned by NEP 2020.

**190.6. Institutional Support Required**

To run educational consultancy effectively, the HEI should have the following support systems:

| **Support Area**              | **Responsibilities**                                                            |
|-------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dean (R&D) / Dean (Academics) | Lead, review, and approve consultancy projects and documentation.               |
| IQAC Cell                     | Align consultancy with quality enhancement and accreditation goals.             |
| Legal Team                    | Draft and review MoUs or contracts with institutions.                           |
| Finance Office                | Manage fund flow, honorariums, and taxation compliance.                         |
| Departments & Faculty Experts | Deliver consultancy in their area of academic or administrative specialization. |

**190.7. Best Practices**

• Clearly define deliverables, responsibilities, and timeframes in every consultancy agreement.

• Maintain confidentiality and IP clauses, especially if proprietary information is involved.

• Ensure the quality and relevance of services delivered.

• Use consultancy outcomes to enhance institutional teaching-learning and research.

• Document and report all consultancy activities for IQAC and accreditation reports.

**191. Community Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

**191.1. Definition**

Community Consultancy refers to the advisory, problem-solving, and capacity-building services provided by Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) to address local community issues. These services are typically non-commercial or low-cost, and are aligned with the institution's social responsibility and extension activities.

The focus is on applying academic knowledge to real-world community problems, thereby bridging the gap between the institution and society.

**191.2. Objectives of Community Consultancy**

| **Objective**         | **Explanation**                                                                          |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Societal Impact       | Help address pressing local issues like health, sanitation, education, agriculture, etc. |
| Social Responsibility | Demonstrate the HEI's commitment to inclusive development.                               |
| Student Engagement    | Involve students in practical, socially relevant projects.                               |
| Knowledge Sharing     | Apply institutional expertise to solve community problems.                               |
| Policy Influence      | Provide data, research, and advice to local authorities or NGOs.                         |

**191.3. Scope of Community Consultancy**

| **Domain**          | **Activities**                                                                                 |
|---------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Rural Development   | Advising on water management, sanitation systems, waste disposal, etc.                         |
| Health and Hygiene  | Organizing medical camps, awareness programs, and health audits.                               |
| Women Empowerment   | Skill training, digital literacy workshops, and self-help group support.                       |
| Education           | Digital Literacy: Supporting local schools with teacher training, curriculum development, etc. |
| Environment         | Tree plantation, eco-clubs, biodiversity audits, pollution control recommendations.            |
| Disaster Management | Awareness training, resource mapping, and emergency response planning.                         |
| Digital Literacy    | Introducing villagers to mobile banking, e-Governance services, or online education.           |

**191.4. Stakeholders Involved**

• Faculty – Provide subject-matter expertise.

• Students – Participate in field visits, data collection, and solution design.

• NGOs / CBOs – Act as intermediaries or partners.

• Government Agencies – Offer support or implement suggested policies.

• Local Panchayats / Urban Bodies – Primary beneficiaries and collaborators.

**191.5. Process of Community Consultancy**

1\. **Problem Identification**

> o Through surveys, field visits, or requests from community leaders.

2\. **Need Assessment**

> o Faculty and students assess the root causes and gather data.

3\. **Proposal Development**

> o Create a plan with deliverables, timelines, and resource needs.

4\. **Community Collaboration**

> o Conduct focus group discussions, meetings, and awareness drives.

5\. **Implementation**

> o Offer technical advice, capacity-building, or create low-cost prototypes.

6\. **Monitoring & Impact Evaluation**

> o Assess the effectiveness and sustainability of the solutions provided.

7\. **Documentation & Reporting**

> o Share outcomes with stakeholders and include in institutional reports (e.g., NAAC).

**191.6. Examples of Community Consultancy Projects**

| **HEI Department**    | **Project**                               | **Community Impact**                      |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Civil Engineering     | Design of rainwater harvesting systems    | Improved groundwater levels in village    |
| Social Sciences       | Survey on drop-out rates in rural schools | Data used for district-level policy       |
| Management            | Digital marketing training for SHGs       | Boosted income of women entrepreneurs     |
| Computer Science      | App for local healthcare appointments     | Streamlined patient access to clinics     |
| Environmental Science | Solid waste management plan               | Cleaner and healthier village environment |

**191.7. Benefits to the HEI**

| **Benefit**              | **Description**                                                           |
|--------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Student Learning         | Hands-on learning through real-world challenges.                          |
| Faculty Engagement       | Interdisciplinary, socially relevant research and service.                |
| Institutional Reputation | Builds the HEI's public image and trust in the community.                 |
| Accreditation Scores     | Supports extension activity and societal engagement criteria in NAAC/NBA. |
| Government Collaboration | Opens doors to CSR funds, district projects, and MoUs with local bodies.  |

**191.8. Institutional Support System Required**

| **Support Cell**             | **Role**                                                  |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Dean (R&D) or Extension Cell | Approves and monitors community consultancy projects.     |
| NSS/NCC Units                | Mobilize students for fieldwork.                          |
| IQAC                         | Keeps records for quality audits and accreditation.       |
| Finance/Legal                | Manages small grants, partnerships, and documentation.    |
| Department Heads             | Align projects with course outcomes and faculty interest. |

**191.9. Best Practices**

• **Participatory Approach:** Involve the community in identifying needs and implementing solutions.

• **Low-Cost, High-Impact:** Focus on frugal innovation and sustainable interventions.

• **Interdisciplinary Teams:** Combine expertise from different departments (e.g., Engineering + Social Work).

• **Documentation:** Keep detailed reports, photos, and testimonials for internal records and accreditation.

• **Follow-Up:** Ensure solutions are maintained and scaled by the community or local bodies.

**192. Technical Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

**192.1. Definition**

Technical Consultancy refers to professional services offered by faculty, departments, or research centers of a Higher Educational Institution (HEI) to external organizations— industries, government agencies, or startups— to solve specific technical problems or improve operational processes using their domain expertise, tools, and infrastructure. This consultancy typically involves:

• Engineering solutions

• Technology deployment

• Lab testing

• Software/hardware development

• System design

• Feasibility studies

It may be fee-based, governed by institutional consultancy policies, and sometimes formalized through MoUs.

**192.2. Objectives of Technical Consultancy**

| **Objective**                   | **Description**                                                                              |
|---------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Problem Solving                 | Provide expert solutions to real-world engineering, scientific, or IT-related problems.      |
| Industry-Academia Collaboration | Strengthen links with industries and build mutually beneficial partnerships.                 |
| Knowledge Transfer              | Translate academic research and innovation into practical applications.                      |
| Revenue Generation              | Earn consultancy income to support research labs, faculty development, and student projects. |
| Skill Enhancement               | Enrich faculty and student exposure to industrial challenges and technologies.               |

**192.3. Scope of Technical Consultancy**

| **Field**                 | **Consultancy Areas**                                                      |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Civil Engineering         | Structural design, soil testing, NDT, construction quality audits          |
| Mechanical Engineering    | Design validation, thermal system analysis, CAD/CAM modeling               |
| Electrical Engineering    | Power quality audit, energy efficiency studies, substation design          |
| Electronics/Telecom       | PCB design, embedded system development, signal testing                    |
| Computer Science/IT       | Software development, app design, data analytics, cybersecurity assessment |
| Environmental Engineering | Pollution control systems, effluent treatment plant (ETP) design           |
| Biotechnology/Chemical    | Process optimization, lab analysis, bio-assay services                     |

**192.4. Typical Clients**

• Private Industries (Manufacturing, IT, Pharma, etc.)

• Government Departments (PWD, Municipalities, Smart Cities)

• Startups and MSMEs

• Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)

• NGOs and R&D Labs

• Agriculture or Health Departments

**192.5. Process of Technical Consultancy**

| **Step**                     | **Description**                                                                                                  |
|------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1\. Request from Client      | Industry or agency contacts HEI with a problem or requirement.                                                   |
| 2\. Feasibility Study        | Initial discussion and assessment by faculty/expert team. Scope of work, timelines, deliverables, budget shared. |
| 3\. Proposal & Quotation     | Scope of work, timelines, deliverables, budget shared.                                                           |
| 4\. MoU/Agreement            | Signed by both parties including terms, confidentiality, and payment.                                            |
| 5\. Project Execution        | Lab testing, design, development, or advisory carried out by faculty/team.                                       |
| 6\. Delivery & Report        | Final deliverables and report submitted to client.                                                               |
| 7\. Payment & Acknowledgment | Fees received and distributed as per consultancy policy.                                                         |

**192.6. Examples of Technical Consultancy Projects**

| **Department** | **Project**                       | **Client**                   |
|----------------|-----------------------------------|------------------------------|
| Civil Engg.    | Bridge Load Test                  | Roads & Buildings Department |
| EEE            | Power Audit of Factory            | Private Manufacturing Unit   |
| CSE            | Custom ERP for Hospital           | Local Government Hospital    |
| Mech Engg.     | Failure Analysis of Machine Parts | PSU Industry                 |
| Biotech        | Water Testing for Contamination   | Rural Municipality           |
| ECE            | IoT Sensor Design                 | Agri-Tech Startup            |

**192.7. Revenue Sharing (Typical Model in HEIs)**

| **Recipient**                | **Share (%)**                           |
|------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| Institution (Overhead)       | 30–40%                                  |
| Consulting Faculty/Team      | 60–70%                                  |
| Departmental Fund (optional) | 5–10% (included in institutional share) |

*Subject to HEI's policy and tax rules.*

**192.8. Institutional Support Required**

| **Office / Cell**          | **Role**                                                                |
|----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dean (R&D)                 | Approves and monitors all technical consultancy activities.             |
| Consultancy Cell / IP Cell | Prepares MoUs, NDAs, manages records, and handles patents if needed.    |
| Finance Section            | Manages quotations, payments, and tax deductions (GST, TDS).            |
| IQAC/NAAC Cell             | Records technical consultancy for institutional data and accreditation. |
| Departments                | Execute and supervise the technical assignments.                        |

**192.9. Best Practices**

• Clearly define Scope of Work (SoW) and deliverables in agreement.

• Ensure confidentiality clauses and handle intellectual property (IP) as per policy.

• Maintain proper records, invoices, and impact assessment reports.

• Provide certificates of completion or acknowledgment from client industries.

• Use the consultancy experience to update curriculum, internships, and student projects.

**192.10. Benefits to the Institution**

• Enhances faculty-industry engagement

• Improves employability of students via exposure to live problems

• Supports ranking and accreditation (NAAC/NIRF/NBA)

• Attracts industry-funded labs and research

• Increases institutional visibility and branding

**193. Advisory / Policy Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

**193.1. Definition**

Advisory or Policy Consultancy involves the contribution of academic experts from Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) toward policy formulation, strategic planning, and decision-making for government bodies, public institutions, NGOs, and even industry associations. It focuses on thought leadership and expert advice in areas such as governance, education, health, technology, urban planning, and social development.

This type of consultancy is influential and knowledge-driven, rather than being purely technical or operational.

**193.2. Objectives of Advisory/Policy Consultancy**

| **Objective**                | **Description**                                                           |
|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Evidence-Based Policymaking  | Support policy development through data, models, and research findings.   |
| Expert Guidance              | Provide insights on complex social, economic, and environmental issues.   |
| Capacity Building            | Strengthen institutions by shaping strategies and governance frameworks.  |
| Influencing Public Discourse | Participate in national/international forums and committees.              |
| Enhancing Public Value       | Align institutional research with national priorities and societal needs. |

**193.3. Scope of Policy Consultancy**

| **Sector**          | **Consultancy Areas**                                                |
|---------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Education           | Curriculum design, digital education policy, NEP implementation      |
| Health              | Public health policy, vaccination strategy, health systems planning  |
| Urban Governance    | Smart city planning, mobility, affordable housing                    |
| Environment         | Climate action plans, EIA frameworks, sustainability policy          |
| Agriculture         | Crop insurance models, farmer welfare schemes, agri-tech integration |
| Industry            | MSME development, digital economy, industrial corridors              |
| Labour & Employment | Skilling frameworks, migration policy, gig economy reforms           |
| Social Justice      | Women's empowerment, child protection, tribal policy inputs          |

**193.4. Who Offers Advisory/Policy Consultancy?**

• Senior faculty (Professors, Deans, Chairs)

• Research Centers / Think Tanks within HEIs

• Interdisciplinary Policy Labs

• National and International Collaborations

**193.5. Typical Clients / Stakeholders**

• Government Departments (Central/State)

• Public Policy Think Tanks (NITI Aayog, RIS, etc.)

• International Agencies (UNDP, WHO, World Bank)

• Industry Chambers (CII, FICCI, NASSCOM)

• NGOs and Civil Society Groups

• Judicial / Parliamentary Committees

**193.6. Advisory Consultancy Process**

| **Step**                | **Description**                                                   |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 1\. Request/Engagement  | Initiated by government or agency, or proposed by the HEI expert. |
| 2\. Problem Framing     | Understanding policy goals, target outcomes, and timelines.       |
| 3\. Research & Analysis | Literature review, data analysis, stakeholder consultations.      |

| 6\. Review & Follow-Up  | Feedback integration and support for implementation monitoring.   |

**194. Consultancy Policy for Higher Educational Institutions**

**194.1. Purpose**

The purpose of this policy is to define the framework for undertaking consultancy services by the faculty, staff, and departments of the institution. It aims to promote the application of academic expertise to address external organizations' challenges while maintaining academic integrity and ensuring fair revenue sharing.

**194.2. Scope**

This policy applies to all faculty members, research staff, and departments involved in consultancy services with government agencies, industries, NGOs, and other organizations, whether paid or unpaid.

**194.3. Definition of Consultancy**

Consultancy is a professional service offered by the institution's faculty and staff based on their expertise to external clients for problem-solving, advice, technical assistance, or specialized services. Consultancy may be of various types, including but not limited to:

• Technical Consultancy

• Educational Consultancy

• Research-Based Consultancy

**194.4. Objectives**

• Encourage faculty and staff to engage in consultancy to apply their expertise.

• Strengthen institutional links with industry, government, and society.

• Generate additional revenue to support academic and research activities.

• Enhance learning opportunities for students through real-world exposure.

• Ensure transparency, accountability, and ethical practices in consultancy.

**194.5. Guidelines and Procedures**

**Initiation and Approval**

• Consultancy work should be formally initiated only after approval by the competent authority (Dean R&D / Principal / Director).

• The consultant faculty/department shall submit a proposal detailing the scope, duration, and financial terms.

• Approval will be based on the institution's capacity, conflict of interest, and compliance with academic responsibilities.

**Engagement and Contract**

• A formal MoU/Agreement must be signed between the institution and the client specifying the deliverables, timeline, fees, confidentiality, and liability.

• Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) generated during consultancy will be governed by the institution's IPR policy.

**Execution**

• Consultancy should not interfere with the faculty's teaching, research, and administrative duties.

• Faculty/staff involved should maintain the highest standards of professionalism, ethics, and confidentiality.

• Regular progress reports should be submitted to the institution and the client as agreed.

**Revenue and Cost Sharing**

• Consultancy revenue received will be shared between the faculty, department, and institution as per the following example distribution (can be customized):

> o Faculty: 60%
>
> o Department: 15%
>
> o Institution (for infrastructure, admin): 25%

• All consultancy revenues must be routed through the institution's finance office to ensure transparency.

**Utilization of Funds**

• Institutional share of consultancy revenue may be used to:

> o Improve laboratory and research infrastructure
>
> o Support academic activities, conferences, and workshops
>
> o Promote student development initiatives

**194.6. Roles and Responsibilities**

| **Role**                             | **Responsibility**                                                                                    |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Dean (R&D) / Consultancy Coordinator | Oversee consultancy policy implementation, approval, coordination, and conflict resolution.           |
| Faculty/Staff                        | Prepare proposals, execute consultancy work professionally, submit reports, and comply with policies. |
| Finance Office                       | Manage consultancy funds, ensure transparent accounting and disbursement.                             |
| Legal/Administration                 | Facilitate MoU agreements, ensure compliance with institutional and legal norms.                      |

**194.7. Ethical Considerations**

• Faculty/staff should avoid conflicts of interest and not exploit institutional resources for personal gain beyond the approved consultancy.

• Consultancy should not involve any activity against institutional interests or academic freedom.

• Confidentiality of client data and intellectual property must be strictly maintained.

**194.8. Dispute Resolution**

• Any disputes arising from consultancy work will be resolved amicably by the Dean (R&D) or an appointed committee.

• Legal recourse will be considered only after exhausting institutional mechanisms.

**194.9. Review and Amendment**

• This policy shall be reviewed every two years or as needed.

• Amendments can be proposed by the Dean (R&D) and approved by the institutional governing body.

**194.10. Effective Date**

This policy is effective from \[Date\] and supersedes all previous consultancy guidelines.

**195. Mapping of Consultancy in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) to NAAC Criteria**

Consultancy activities in HEIs significantly contribute to NAAC Accreditation, primarily under Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension. These activities demonstrate the institution's engagement with industry, government, and society, showcasing its ability to apply academic knowledge to solve real-world problems while generating revenue and impact.

**195.1. Key NAAC Criteria Linked to Consultancy**

| **NAAC Criterion**                                 | **Key Metric**                                                                                                                                   |
|----------------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension | 3.4.1: Extension activities in the neighbourhood community in terms of impact and sensitising students to social issues and holistic development |
| Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension | 3.4.3: Number of extension and outreach programs conducted with industry, community, and NGOs                                                    |
| Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension | 3.5.1: Number of functional MoUs with institutions, industries, corporate houses, etc. during the last five years                                |
| Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension | 3.6.3: Number of extension and outreach programs conducted by the institution                                                                    |
| Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension | 3.7.1: Institution has collaboration with other agencies for research/ consultancy/ extension activities                                         |

*Consultancy Relevance notes (per metric, in order above): if consultancy is community-based (e.g., technical help to villages, NGOs), it contributes here; involvement in consultancy for social or environmental good can be documented here; consultancy MoUs with industries and government bodies are counted; particularly relevant for community consultancy or policy advisory projects; reflects on technical, educational, and policy consultancies with external agencies.*

|----------------------------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

To effectively map consultancy activities in NAAC, the following documents are required:

**195.4. Best Practices for NAAC Documentation**

• Maintain a Consultancy Register department-wise.

• Showcase consultancy diversity: technical, educational, policy, community.

**198. Innovation and Incubation in Higher Educational Institutes (HEIs)**

Innovation and Incubation are crucial pillars in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) to foster entrepreneurship, encourage research-based problem-solving, and promote collaboration between academia, industry, and the startup ecosystem.

**198.1. What is Innovation and Incubation?**

**Innovation:** Innovation in HEIs refers to the creation or improvement of products, processes, services, or technologies that offer new or enhanced value. It can be academic, technological, social, or commercial in nature.

Types of Innovations in HEIs:

• Academic Innovation: New teaching-learning practices, curriculum enhancements.

• Technological Innovation: New software, devices, or technical solutions.

• Social Innovation: Community-based problem-solving (e.g., water purification in villages).

• Business Innovation: Startup ideas solving real-world challenges.

**Incubation:** Incubation is the support process offered by an institution to nurture startup ideas and transform them into viable businesses. Institutions often establish Incubation Centres, Innovation Cells, or Entrepreneurship Development Cells (EDCs) for this purpose.

Services Provided by Incubators:

• Physical space (office/lab)

• Mentorship and expert guidance

• Seed funding or access to investors

• Networking opportunities

• Legal/IPR support

• Business plan development

• Training and workshops

**198.2. Objectives of Innovation and Incubation Cells in HEIs**

1\. Foster a culture of creativity, research, and entrepreneurship.

2\. Convert innovative ideas into prototypes, patents, or businesses.

3\. Bridge the gap between academia and industry.

4\. Generate employment and self-employment opportunities.

5\. Support government initiatives like Startup India, Atal Innovation Mission, etc.

**198.3. Key Structures in HEIs for Innovation and Incubation**

| **Structure**                           | **Description**                                                         |
|-----------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Institute Innovation Council (IIC)      | Set up under MoE's Innovation Cell to streamline innovation activities. |
| Entrepreneurship Development Cell (EDC) | Focuses on training and developing student entrepreneurs.               |
| Business Incubation Centre (BIC)        | Offers incubation support, co-working space, seed fund access.          |
| Technology Business Incubator (TBI)     | Govt-funded centers focusing on high-tech and deeptech startups.        |
| Startup Cell                            | Supports student-led startups with mentoring, funding, and networking.  |

**198.4. Innovation & Incubation Activities in HEIs**

• Idea/thesis-to-product transformation

• Hackathons, Ideathons, Startup Bootcamps

• Pre-incubation and acceleration programs

• Industry-academia research collaboration

• Patent filing and IPR training

• Internships in startups and innovation labs

• Student entrepreneurship policy implementation

**198.5. Mapping to National Frameworks**

• NAAC

• NBA

• NIRF

• ARIIA (Atal Ranking of Institutions on Innovation Achievements)

**198.6. Key Performance Indicators**

• Number of startups/incubated ventures

• Patents filed and granted

• Funding received by startups

• Number of student/faculty entrepreneurs

• IPRs and technology transfer cases

• Industry collaborations for innovation

**198.7. Government & Regulatory Bodies Supporting Innovation in HEIs**

• DST – NIDHI, TBI support

**198.8. Benefits to the Institution**

• Industry partnerships and collaborative research

• Revenue generation through licensing or equity in startups

• Enhanced student employability and innovation culture

**199. Academic Research in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs)**

Academic Research in Higher Educational Institutions (HEIs) is a foundational pillar for knowledge creation, innovation, and national development. It involves systematic investigation undertaken by faculty, researchers, and students to contribute to the body of academic knowledge in diverse disciplines.

**199.1. Objectives of Academic Research in HEIs**

1\. **Advance Knowledge:** Discover new theories, models, methods, or data.

2\. **Solve Societal Problems:** Address local, national, and global challenges.

3\. **Enhance Teaching:** Integrate new findings into curriculum and pedagogy.

4\. Promote Innovation and Entrepreneurship.

5\. **Support Policy and Practice:** Contribute to evidence-based decision-making.

6\. **Develop Skills:** Critical thinking, data analysis, and communication among students and scholars.

**199.2. Types of Academic Research in HEIs**

| **Type**                        | **Description**                                                                |
|---------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Basic (Fundamental) Research    | Focused on understanding fundamental principles without immediate application. |
| Applied Research                | Aimed at solving specific practical problems or developing products.           |
| Action Research                 | Conducted to improve practices within educational or organizational settings.  |
| Interdisciplinary Research      | Involves collaboration across multiple academic fields.                        |
| Collaborative/Industry Research | Conducted in partnership with industries or research organizations.            |

**199.3. Key Stakeholders in Academic Research**

• Faculty Members: Principal investigators leading research projects.

• Research Scholars (Ph.D./M.Phil): Engaged in long-term academic research.

• PG and UG Students: Involved in mini-projects, thesis work, internships.

• Research Centres: Dedicated centers of excellence or domain-specific labs.

• Funding Agencies: DST, UGC, CSIR, ICSSR, DBT, AICTE, DRDO, ISRO, etc.

**199.4. Research Components in HEIs**

• Research Proposals & Projects

• Publications (Journals, Conferences, Books)

• Patents and IPR

• Research Collaborations (national/international)

• Thesis & Dissertation Supervision

• Research Ethics and Plagiarism Check

• Research Data Management

• Capacity Building (FDPs, Workshops)

**199.5. Infrastructure for Academic Research**

• Dedicated research labs with modern equipment

• Digital libraries and access to databases (IEEE, Scopus, JSTOR, etc.)

• High-speed internet and computing facilities

• Institutional Research Committee / Ethics Committee

• Sponsored Research & Industrial Consultancy Cell (SRIC/IRC)

**199.6. Research Promotion Strategies in HEIs**

1\. Establishing Research and Development (R&D) Cells.

2\. Providing seed funding for faculty-led research.

3\. Offering research incentives (publication awards, patent support).

4\. Organizing conferences, workshops, and FDPs.

5\. Encouraging faculty-student research collaboration.

6\. Linking research with community development and curriculum.

7\. Promoting interdisciplinary and translational research.

**199.7. Mapping to NAAC / NBA / NIRF / ARIIA**

| **Framework** | **Role of Academic Research**                                                                   |
|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| NAAC          | Criterion III: Research, Innovations and Extension (Research projects, publications, IPR, MoUs) |
| NBA           | Program Outcome 4: Conduct investigations of complex problems using research-based knowledge    |
| NIRF          | ‘Research and Professional Practice’ (RP) – publications, quality of research, patents          |
| ARIIA         | Measures innovation-based research, startup activity, and funding                               |

**199.8. Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)**

• Number and quality of publications (indexed in Scopus, WoS)

• Citation metrics (h-index, i10-index)

• Number of funded projects and grants received

• Patents filed/granted

• Collaborative research projects (national/international)

• Revenue from consultancy and research commercialization

• Number of PhDs produced

**199.9. Benefits of Academic Research**

• Builds institutional reputation and global visibility.

• Drives curriculum updates aligned with emerging knowledge.

• Enhances faculty development and student learning.

• Attracts external funding and industry collaboration.

• Contributes to socio-economic development.

**200. Seed Funding in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)**

**200.1. Definition and Purpose**

• Seed funding refers to early-stage financial support provided to student or faculty start-ups to develop a proof of concept (PoC) or prototype.

• It helps bridge the gap between idea generation and commercial viability.

• Enables campus start-ups to validate product-market fit, hire initial team members, and build MVPs (Minimum Viable Products).

**200.2. Sources of Seed Funding in HEIs**

*A. Government Schemes*

• **Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS – DPIIT):**

> o ₹20 lakhs for validation, ₹50 lakhs for scaling
>
> o Available through recognized campus incubators

• **NIDHI-PRAYAS (DST):**

> o Up to ₹10 lakhs per idea for hardware-based innovations

• **MSME Innovative Scheme:**

> o ₹15 lakhs per idea for student/faculty MSME projects

• **TIDE 2.0 (MeitY):**

> o ₹4–7 lakhs for tech-based PoCs

*B. Institutional Grants*

• Internal Innovation and Entrepreneurship Development Funds

• Alumni-sponsored innovation grants

• CSR funds from industry partners for student ventures

*C. Private and Industry Partnerships*

• Corporate-sponsored seed grants (e.g., Intel, Google, Bosch)

• Startup accelerators and VCs engaging with HEI incubators (e.g., 100X.VC, Indian Angel Network)

**200.3. Eligibility Criteria**

• Start-up should be incubated within the HEI or through its incubator.

• Must be student, faculty, or alumni-led.

• Should have an innovative, scalable, and socially relevant idea.

• Business plan or pitch deck is usually required.

**200.4. Components Covered**

• Prototype development

• Product design and testing

• Market research and customer validation

• Initial team support and office space

• IP filing, legal, and incorporation costs

**200.5. Institutional Support Mechanisms**

• Startup Selection Committee to evaluate seed fund proposals.

• Mentoring and guidance through IIC or Incubation Centre.

• Regular demo days and investor pitch sessions.

• Access to technical labs and shared resources.

**200.6. Impact of Seed Funding in HEIs**

• Enables student entrepreneurs to launch their ventures directly from campus.

• Boosts startup survival rate beyond ideation stage.

• Enhances HEI performance in ARIIA, NIRF innovation rankings, and NAAC criteria.

• Encourages patenting, product launches, and job creation.

**200.7. Challenges and Solutions**

• Lack of awareness:

> o Solution: Conduct seed fund orientation and proposal writing workshops.

• Improper utilization:

> o Solution: Implement milestone-based disbursement and auditing.

• Short funding window:

> o Solution: Combine multiple schemes or promote follow-on funding opportunities.

**200.8. Seed Funding Evaluation Rubric (Total Score: 100 Points)**

**1. Innovativeness of the Idea (20 points)**

• Truly novel and disruptive innovation – 16–20 points

• Moderate innovation, with some differentiation – 11–15 points

• Common or marginally improved idea – 6–10 points

• Minimal innovation – 0–5 points

**2. Problem-Solution Fit (15 points)**

• Clearly addresses a real, validated problem with measurable impact – 13–15 points

• Identifies a relevant problem, some validation done – 9–12 points

• Vague problem definition or unclear relevance – 5–8 points

• Problem poorly defined – 0–4 points

**3. Market Potential (15 points)**

• Large, growing, and well-defined market with evident demand – 13–15 points

• Moderate market size, some validation – 9–12 points

• Niche or uncertain market – 5–8 points

• No clear market – 0–4 points

**4. Feasibility & Implementation Plan (15 points)**

• Realistic timeline, clear milestones, and sound technical approach – 13–15 points

• Feasible but lacking detailed execution plan – 9–12 points

• Vague or weak implementation strategy – 5–8 points

• No clarity on feasibility – 0–4 points

**5. Team Composition & Capability (10 points)**

• Diverse, experienced, and committed team – 9–10 points

• Capable team with some relevant expertise – 6–8 points

• Limited experience or incomplete team – 3–5 points

• Solo founder or unclear roles – 0–2 points

**6. Prototype / PoC Status (10 points)**

• Working prototype or PoC already built – 9–10 points

• Prototype under development – 6–8 points

• Design/concept only – 3–5 points

• No progress beyond idea – 0–2 points

**7. Scalability and Sustainability (10 points)**

• High potential for scaling and long-term sustainability – 9–10 points

• Moderate scalability with some risks – 6–8 points

• Niche with limited scale – 3–5 points

• No scalability potential – 0–2 points

**8. Social/Environmental Impact (5 points)** *(Optional bonus)*

• Strong positive social or environmental contribution – 5 points

• Some impact but not primary focus – 3–4 points

• Minimal or no visible impact – 0–2 points

Selection Threshold Recommendation

• 75–100: High potential – *Recommend for full seed funding*

• 60–74: Medium potential – *Recommend with modifications or reduced funding*

• Below 60: Low priority – *Not eligible in current form*
