**212.6. Technology Transfer and Industry Linkages**

• DRDO provides technologies to PSUs (like HAL, BDL, BEL) and private industries

• Encourages participation of MSMEs and startups

• Through its “DRDO – Technology Development Fund (TDF)”, it supports industrial partners in developing components/systems

**212.7. Academic and Student Engagement**

• DIAT (Defence Institute of Advanced Technology) in Pune – A deemed university under DRDO

• DRDO Research Fellowships (JRF, SRF, RA) – For students in STEM fields

• Extramural Research – Funded projects in academic institutions

• Student Internships and Projects – Short-term training in DRDO labs

**212.8. International Collaborations**

DRDO collaborates with global partners including:

• Russia (e.g., BrahMos JV)

• Israel (missile defense systems)

• USA, France, UK, South Korea on various tech projects

**212.9. Initiatives for Self-Reliance**

• Make in India in Defence

• Indigenization of Strategic Components

• Private Sector Participation in defense production

• iDEX (Innovations for Defence Excellence) platform for startups and innovators

• Technology Development Fund (TDF) to promote dual-use technology development

**212.10. Awards and Recognition**

DRDO scientists and teams have received:

• Padma Awards

• Agni Award for Excellence in Self-Reliance

• Defence Technology Spin-Off Awards for civil applications of military technology

**212.11. Examples of DRDO Spin-Off Technologies**

• Bio-digesters (Tech) – Railway toilets (Civilian Use)

• Bulletproof jackets (Tech) – civilian/law-enforcement use

• High-nutrition food (Tech) – civilian use

• Water purification kits (Tech) – civilian use

**212.12. Key Research Funding Schemes**

• Extramural Research (ER) Scheme:

> o Provides financial support for faculty-led defence R&D projects in HEIs.

• Technology Development Fund (TDF) (via DRDO and MoD):

> o For development of defence technologies by academia and MSMEs.

• Research Boards under DRDO:

> o ARMREB – Armaments Research Board
>
> o NRB – Naval Research Board
>
> o AERB – Aeronautics Research Board
>
> o LRB – Life Sciences Research Board
>
> o JCB – Joint Communication Board

**212.13. Focus Areas**

• Artificial Intelligence (AI), Robotics, and Cybersecurity

• Missile Guidance, Radar Systems, Avionics

• High-Energy Materials, Explosives, and Propulsion

• Stealth Technology, Materials Science, Nanotechnology

• Biodefence and Life Sciences

• Quantum Technologies, UAVs, and Underwater Systems

**212.14. Eligible Institutions**

• AICTE/UGC-approved technical institutions (IITs, NITs, IIITs, state/private universities).

• Institutions with proven R&D capacity and infrastructure.

• Faculty with a strong research track record in relevant domains.

**212.15. Funding and Support**

• Typical project duration: 1 to 3 years.

• Funding covers:

> o Research staff (JRF/SRF/RA) salaries
>
> o Equipment, software, testing facilities
>
> o Consumables and contingency
>
> o Travel and dissemination

• Some schemes may involve technology incubation and prototyping phases.

**212.16. Monitoring and Compliance**

• Periodic technical review meetings and site inspections by DRDO.

• Progress reports, financial audits, and UCs must be submitted.

• Confidentiality and IPR agreements signed by institutions.

**212.17. Outcomes and Expectations**

• Development of indigenous technologies with direct defence application.

• Publications (where permitted), patents, or prototypes.

• Possibility of technology transfer or further development by DRDO labs.

• Skill development of students and researchers in critical tech areas.

**212.18. Institutional Benefits**

• Enhances institutional profile in national-level R&D.

• Access to classified research domains and collaboration with DRDO labs.

• Opportunity to contribute to Atmanirbhar Bharat in defence.

• Establishment of CoEs or DRDO Industry-Academia Centres of Excellence.

**213. ISRO (Indian Space Research Organization) Sponsored Research in Higher Education Institutions**

**213.1. Introduction**

The Indian Space Research Organization (ISRO) is India's national space agency, functioning under the Department of Space, Government of India. It is globally recognized for cost-effective, indigenous, and innovative space missions that serve both strategic and societal goals.

• **Established:** 15 August 1969

• **Founder:** Dr. Vikram Sarabhai (Father of India’s Space Program)

• **Headquarters:** Bengaluru, Karnataka

**213.2. Primary Objectives of ISRO**

1\. Develop space technology and its application for national tasks

2\. Design and launch satellites for communication, earth observation, and navigation

3\. Conduct space science research and planetary exploration

4\. Support tele-education, telemedicine, disaster management, and agriculture

5\. Enhance international collaboration and private sector involvement

**213.3. Key Program Areas**

| **Area**                      | **Focus**                                                                                |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Satellite Communication**   | GSAT series, INSAT, broadband, mobile networks                                           |
| **Earth Observation**         | Cartosat, Oceansat, Resourcesat, RISAT                                                   |
| **Navigation**                | IRNSS/NavIC (India’s GPS equivalent)                                                     |
| **Space Science**             | Chandrayaan, Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan), Aditya-L1                                |
| **Launch Vehicles**           | PSLV, GSLV, SSLV, LVM-3                                                                  |
| **Human Spaceflight**         | Gaganyaan program                                                                        |
| **International Cooperation** | Launch of foreign satellites, collaborations with NASA, ESA, JAXA, Roscosmos, CNES, etc. |

**213.4. Major Launch Vehicles**

| **Vehicle**            | **Details**                                                              |
|------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **PSLV**               | Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle – workhorse for remote sensing satellites |
| **GSLV**               | Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle – used for heavier payloads      |
| **GSLV Mk III / LVM3** | Heavy-lift vehicle for crewed missions and deep space                    |
| **SSLV**               | Small Satellite Launch Vehicle – for quick, low-cost deployment          |

**213.5. Notable Missions**

| **Mission**                                 | **Description**                                                           |
|---------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Chandrayaan-1 (2008)**                    | India's 1st lunar mission; discovered water on the Moon                   |
| **Chandrayaan-2 (2019)**                    | Orbiter successful; lander lost during descent                            |
| **Chandrayaan-3 (2023)**                    | Successful lunar landing at the south pole – global milestone             |
| **Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission, 2013)** | First Asian country to reach Mars orbit on the first attempt              |
| **Aditya-L1 (2023)**                        | First Indian solar mission – studying solar corona from Lagrange point L1 |
| **XPoSat (2024)**                           | India’s first dedicated astronomy mission to study X-ray polarization     |
| **Gaganyaan (Upcoming)**                    | India’s first human spaceflight mission (crew module already tested)      |

**213.6. Satellite Programs**

1\. INSAT/GSAT

• Telecommunications, TV broadcasting, meteorology, disaster alerts

2\. IRS (Indian Remote Sensing) Satellites

• Earth observation, agriculture, forestry, urban planning, water resources

3\. NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation)

• India's independent GPS system covering the Indian subcontinent

**213.7. Space Applications for Societal Development**

• Telemedicine & Tele-education through satellites

• Disaster Monitoring using real-time data (cyclones, earthquakes, floods)

• Agricultural Forecasting & crop yield estimation

• Fisheries & Marine Resources mapping

• Village Resource Centres for rural support

• Smart governance through GIS mapping

**213.8. ISRO and Industry Collaboration**

• ISRO increasingly involves private industries and startups for:

> o Satellite manufacturing
>
> o Launch vehicle parts
>
> o Ground support systems
>
> o Technology transfer

• **NewSpace India Ltd (NSIL):** Facilitates commercial exploitation of ISRO’s products

• **IN-SPACe (Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Center):** Single-window clearance for private players to use ISRO infrastructure

**213.9. Academic and Research Opportunities**

• IIRS (Indian Institute of Remote Sensing) – Training in geospatial sciences

• IIST (Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology) – Deemed university under ISRO

• **RESPOND Projects** – ISRO funds academic R&D on space tech

• Student Satellite Programs – Collaboration with universities (e.g., ANUSAT, STUDSAT)

• Internships, JRFs, and Research Fellowships

**213.10. Commercial Arm and Startups**

• Antrix Corporation – ISRO's original commercial arm

• NSIL (NewSpace India Ltd) – Now the primary commercial body

• IN-SPACe – Promotes and regulates private sector participation

• **Notable Private Collaborations:** Skyroot Aerospace, Agnikul Cosmos, Pixxel, Dhruva Space

**213.11. ISRO’s Global Recognition**

• Launched over 400 foreign satellites from 35+ countries

• Known for cost-effective missions (e.g., Mars mission at 1/10th the cost of NASA)

• Recognized by NASA, ESA, and other global agencies for data and collaboration

**213.12. International Collaborations**

• USA (NASA) – NISAR mission (earth observation satellite)

• France (CNES) – Megha-Tropiques, SARAL

• Russia – Crew module cooperation for Gaganyaan

• Japan (JAXA) – Lunar and planetary exploration

• European Space Agency (ESA) – Data exchange, training

**213.13. Spin-off Technologies**

| **Field**               | **Application**                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------|
| **Weather forecasting** | Cyclone and flood warning systems       |
| **Telecommunication**   | VSAT and DTH tech                       |
| **Navigation**          | Tracking logistics, disaster relief     |
| **Agriculture**         | Crop planning, pest surveillance        |
| **Medicine**            | Telemedicine units for rural healthcare |
| **Urban Planning**      | Satellite-based land use mapping        |

**213.14. Key Research Support Schemes**

• RESPOND (Research Sponsored) Programme:

> o Flagship program funding R&D in space science, satellite tech, propulsion, etc.
>
> o Open to faculty from AICTE/UGC-recognised institutions.

• ISRO-UNNATI Program:

> o Hands-on training for faculty and students in nano-satellite design and applications.

• Space Technology Cells (STCs):

> o Established in top-tier HEIs (e.g., IITs, IISc) to act as nodal points for ISRO research.

• Young Scientist Research Programme:

> o Supports postgraduates and PhD scholars working on space-related topics.

**213.15. Priority Research Areas**

• Remote Sensing and GIS Applications

• Satellite Communication and Navigation

• Spacecraft Design and Propulsion

• Payload Development and Testing

• Data Analytics, AI/ML for Space Missions

• Space Weather, Astrophysics, and Planetary Science

**213.16. Eligible Institutions and Researchers**

• Engineering colleges, science universities, and national institutes.

• Faculty members with relevant expertise and research record.

• Institutions must have basic infrastructure and lab facilities for execution.

**213.17. Funding and Support**

• Support for:

> o Research staff (JRF/SRF/RA)
>
> o Equipment, simulation tools, and lab setups
>
> o Travel and contingency
>
> o Publication and dissemination

• Duration: Typically 2–3 years.

• Amount: Project-based (usually ₹10–30 lakhs per project).

**213.18. Application and Evaluation Process**

• Proposals submitted through ISRO’s RESPOND portal or via Space Technology Cells.

• Proposal includes:

> o Research objective, literature review, methodology, work plan, and budget.
>
> o Institutional endorsement and PI bio-data.

• Evaluation by ISRO domain experts and scientists.

• Selection based on scientific merit and relevance to space missions.

**213.19. Monitoring and Compliance**

• Quarterly/annual progress reports and utilization certificates (UCs).

• Review meetings by ISRO’s technical committees.

• Final technical and financial reports after project closure.

**213.20. Outcomes and Expectations**

• Development of prototypes, algorithms, or models useful for ISRO missions.

• Academic outputs like research papers, patents, and conference presentations.

• Potential for student internships and collaborative missions with ISRO centres.

**213.21. Institutional Benefits**

• Enhanced visibility in space research and satellite technology.

• Access to technical guidance and collaboration with ISRO scientists.

• Strengthens institution’s eligibility for future missions and satellite building.

• Opportunity to be part of national innovation initiatives like Gaganyaan, Chandrayaan, Aditya-L1.

**214. DBT (Department of Biotechnology) Sponsored Research in Higher Education Institutions**

**214.1. Objectives of DBT-Sponsored Research in HEIs**

• Promote advanced research and innovation in biotechnology and life sciences.

• Strengthen biotech education and research infrastructure in academic institutions.

• Foster interdisciplinary research and industry-academia collaboration.

• Address national challenges in health, agriculture, environment, and bioresources.

**214.2. Major Research Funding Schemes**

• Research and Development (R&D) Projects:

> o Supports investigator-initiated research proposals in core biotech domains.

• Biotechnology Research Innovation Council (BRIC-BIRAC):

> o Promotes translational research through industry-academia partnerships.

• DBT-BUILDER Programme:

> o Strengthens biotechnology infrastructure in HEIs.

• DBT-STAR College Scheme:

> o Supports undergraduate life science programs in colleges.

• DBT Postgraduate Teaching Programs:

> o Funds M.Sc./M.Tech courses in biotechnology across HEIs.

• Twinning and Inter-Institutional Programs:

> o Bridges gaps between elite and resource-limited institutions.

• Ramalingaswami Re-entry Fellowship / DBT-Wellcome India Alliance:

> o Attracts young scientists back to Indian HEIs for long-term biotech research.

**214.3. Priority Research Areas**

• Genomics, Proteomics, and Molecular Biology

• Agricultural Biotechnology and GM Crops

• Industrial Biotechnology and Enzyme Technology

• Vaccine Development and Molecular Diagnostics

• Environmental Biotechnology and Waste Management

• Stem Cells, Regenerative Medicine, and Neuroscience

**214.4. Eligible Institutions**

• UGC/AICTE-approved universities, colleges, and research institutes.

• Institutions with life sciences, biotech, pharmacy, or allied departments.

• Faculty and researchers with prior research experience or early-career investigators.

**214.5. Funding and Support**

• Covers:

> o Research fellowships (JRF/SRF/RA) and technical staff
>
> o Equipment, reagents, and consumables
>
> o Travel, workshops, publications, and overheads

• Typical project duration: 2–3 years.

• Budget range: ₹20 lakhs to ₹1 crore+ depending on scheme and scope.

**214.6. Application Process**

• Proposals invited via DBT online portal (eProMIS): https://dbtepromis.gov.in

• Components:

> o Background, objectives, methodology, deliverables
>
> o Budget justification and institutional endorsement

• Reviewed by subject expert panels and technical committees.

**214.7. Monitoring and Evaluation**

• Half-yearly or annual progress reports.

• Mid-term review and final presentation to DBT panels.

• Utilization certificates and impact assessment after project closure.

**214.8. Outcomes and Expectations**

• High-impact publications, patents, and commercial technologies.

• Enhanced teaching and research infrastructure in biotechnology.

• Development of bio-based solutions for agriculture, health, and sustainability.

• Human resource development in cutting-edge biotech domains.

**214.9. Institutional Benefits**

• Builds long-term partnerships with national biotech networks (e.g., BIRAC, NIBMG).

• Improves NAAC/NIRF scores through research outcomes.

• Enables student participation in research and biotech start-ups.

• Opportunity to evolve into Centre of Excellence (CoE) in Biotechnology.

**215. ICSSR (Indian Council of Social Science Research) Sponsored Research in Higher Education Institutions**

**215.1. Objectives of ICSSR-Sponsored Research in HEIs**

• Promote high-quality research in social sciences addressing national development.

• Support faculty and scholars in conducting research on social, economic, and political issues.

• Encourage interdisciplinary and policy-relevant studies.

• Strengthen research infrastructure and capabilities in social science departments of HEIs.

**215.2. Major Research Funding Schemes**

• Major Research Projects (MRP):

> o For senior scholars; funding up to ₹15–20 lakhs.

• Minor Research Projects (MiRP):

> o For early-career faculty; funding up to ₹5–7 lakhs.

• ICSSR Doctoral Fellowship:

> o For full-time PhD scholars in recognized HEIs.

• Post-Doctoral Fellowship (PDF):

> o For recent PhD holders to pursue independent research.

• Senior Fellowship:

> o For experienced scholars with proven academic records.

• Short-term Empirical Research Projects:

> o For time-bound field studies on emerging issues.

• Research Surveys and Exploratory Studies (RSES):

> o Funding for state-of-the-art literature surveys and research gap identification.

**215.3. Priority Research Areas**

• Economics, Political Science, Sociology, and History

• Education, Psychology, Public Policy, and Gender Studies

• Social Exclusion, Tribal Studies, and Rural Development

• Law, Media, Environment, and Globalisation

• Contemporary Socio-political and Economic Issues

**215.4. Eligible Institutions and Researchers**

• HEIs recognized by UGC/AICTE, including central/state/private universities.

• Faculty members with a PhD in social sciences.

• Preference given to NAAC/NIRF-accredited institutions.

• Affiliated research institutes and centres with ICSSR recognition.

**215.5. Funding and Support**

• Covers:

> o Honorarium/stipend for researchers (especially in fellowships).
>
> o Fieldwork expenses, travel, and data collection.
>
> o Research assistance, contingencies, and library resources.
>
> o Publication and dissemination support.

• Project duration: 12 to 24 months (depending on type).

• Budget varies by scheme: ₹5 lakhs to ₹20 lakhs.

**215.6. Application Process**

• Application via ICSSR online portal: https://icssr.org

• Proposal must include:

> o Research rationale, objectives, literature review, and methodology.
>
> o Timeframe, budget estimate, and expected outcomes.
>
> o Institutional and ethical clearance where necessary.

• Evaluated by subject experts and screening committees.

**215.7. Monitoring and Evaluation**

• Quarterly/biannual progress reports.

• Mid-term reviews for long-duration projects.

• Final project report and financial utilization certificate (UC) required.

• Publications to acknowledge ICSSR funding support.

**215.8. Outcomes and Expectations**

• Policy-relevant findings to aid national and regional decision-making.

• Research publications, working papers, and monographs.

• Enhanced capacity of social science researchers.

• Development of institutional research culture.

**215.9. Institutional Benefits**

• Improved research reputation in social sciences.

• Eligibility to become ICSSR-recognised research centres.

• Greater visibility in policy discourse and think tank networks.

• Strengthened interdisciplinary collaboration and funding access.

**216. MSMEs (Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises) in Higher Education Institutions**

**216.1. Objective of Promoting MSMEs in HEIs**

• Foster entrepreneurial culture among students and faculty.

• Facilitate industry-academia collaboration with MSMEs for innovation and R&D.

• Enable technology transfer, incubation, and start-up creation from HEI research.

• Support local and national economic development through knowledge-based enterprises.

**216.2. Key Government Schemes Supporting MSMEs in HEIs**

• Support for Entrepreneurial and Managerial Development of SMEs through Incubators (by Ministry of MSME):

> o Financial aid for converting student ideas into viable MSME units.

• MSME Innovative Scheme:

> o Offers funding for incubation, design, and IPR for ideas emerging from HEIs.

• Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Startups (CGSS):

> o Financial risk mitigation for HEI-supported start-ups/MSMEs.

• Technology Centres and Tool Rooms (MSME ministry-affiliated):

> o Provide technical training, tooling, and prototyping support to HEIs and MSMEs.

**216.3. Roles of HEIs in MSME Development**

• Business Incubation Centres and Technology Business Incubators (TBIs):

> o Help in ideation, prototyping, and launching MSME-based start-ups.

• Entrepreneurship Development Cells (EDCs):

> o Conduct workshops, mentoring, and skill training programs.

• Live Industry Projects and Consultancy:

> o Students and faculty offer tech and management solutions to MSMEs.

• Joint R&D and Product Development:

> o Collaborative projects between MSMEs and HEI researchers.

**216.4. Benefits to Students and Faculty**

• Opportunity to commercialize innovations via MSME route.

• Access to seed funding, mentorship, and industrial exposure.

• Enhanced employability and self-reliance.

• Potential for co-founding start-ups or working in research-intensive MSMEs.

**216.5. Institutional Advantages**

• Recognition as MSME-supporting innovation hubs.

• Improved performance in NAAC/NIRF and ARIIA rankings.

• Increased opportunity for funding and partnership with government and industry.

• Strengthens local economic development and community outreach.

**216.6. Challenges and Solutions**

• Limited awareness among students/faculty:

> o Conduct regular entrepreneurship awareness camps (EACs).

• Weak industry linkage:

> o Build MSME-HEI partnership platforms and MoUs.

• Funding access for early-stage ventures:

> o Tap into MSME Ministry, DST, and DBT incubation grants.

• Commercialisation gaps:

> o Train students in IPR, business planning, and market research.

**216.7. Examples of Successful Models**

• IITs and NITs supporting MSMEs through CoEs and TBIs.

• Rural Technology Business Incubators aiding MSMEs in agriculture and handicrafts.

• Polytechnic colleges offering technical consultancy and machine testing to nearby MSMEs.

**217. Model Framework for Setting Up an MSME Incubation Cell in a Higher Education Institution**

**217.1. Vision and Mission**

• **Vision:** To foster innovation, entrepreneurship, and MSME development through academic-industry collaboration.

• **Mission:** To support idea-to-market pathways by enabling student/faculty-led start-ups and providing incubation support to MSMEs.

**217.2. Governance Structure**

• Incubation Advisory Committee (IAC):

> o Chairperson (Dean/Principal)
>
> o MSME representative
>
> o Industry expert
>
> o Incubation Manager
>
> o Faculty experts (science/engineering/management)

• Incubation Cell Coordinator:

> o Reports to IAC
>
> o Manages day-to-day operations

**217.3. Physical Infrastructure**

• Incubation Space:

> o 1000–3000 sq. ft. with co-working space, meeting rooms, and lab access

• Facilities:

> o High-speed internet, workstations
>
> o Shared services: printers, conference room, admin support

• Access to labs and workshops:

> o Engineering, design, biotech, or computer science labs

**217.4. Core Functions**

• Idea Screening & Selection:

> o Quarterly calls for proposals from students/faculty
>
> o Evaluation based on innovation, feasibility, and MSME potential

• Mentoring & Training:

> o Regular workshops on entrepreneurship, business planning, IPR, compliance
>
> o One-on-one mentoring sessions with domain experts

• Funding & Support:

> o Leverage schemes like:
>
> o MSME Innovative Scheme
>
> o DST-NIDHI-PRAYAS
>
> o AICTE SPICES/TBI
>
> o Connect with angel investors or local banks for seed capital

• Industry Collaboration:

> o MoUs with MSMEs for:
>
> o Joint R&D
>
> o Student internships
>
> o Consultancy services

• IPR and Commercialisation:

> o Support in patent filing, licensing, and tech transfer

**217.5. Operational Model**

• Tenure for Incubatees:

> o 12–24 months (extendable based on progress)

• Revenue Model:

> o Nominal monthly rental or equity-sharing option
>
> o Project-based consultancy fee from MSMEs

• Performance Metrics:

> o No. of start-ups incubated
>
> o MSME linkages established
>
> o Patents filed and products launched

**217.6. Partnerships & Stakeholders**

• Government:

> o MSME Ministry, DST, DBT, AICTE, UGC

• Industry:

> o CII, FICCI, local industrial associations

• Academia:

> o Tie-ups with nearby technical and management institutions

• Support Agencies:

> o SIDBI, NSIC, NABARD, Startup India

**217.7. Sustainability Plan**

• Institutional funding for the first 2 years

• Gradual revenue generation from:

> o Consultancy services
>
> o Incubation fees
>
> o Industry-sponsored R&D

• Apply for recognition as a Host Institute under MSME incubation scheme

**217.8. Outcomes and Impact**

• 10–15 incubated start-ups in 3 years

• 30+ student innovations supported annually

• MoUs with at least 10 MSMEs

• Creation of jobs, IP, and community-based enterprises

**218. NABARD (National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development) in Higher Education Institutions**

**218.1. Objectives of NABARD Involvement in HEIs**

• Promote agri-rural innovation, sustainable development, and entrepreneurship.

• Support rural-oriented research and capacity building in agriculture, agri-business, and rural development.

• Encourage student and faculty engagement in rural outreach and development projects.

• Facilitate collaboration between academia and rural institutions/MSMEs.

**218.2. Key Areas of Engagement**

• Research and Development (R&D) Funding:

> o Grants for applied research in agriculture, water management, climate resilience, etc.

• Rural Entrepreneurship Development Cells (REDCs):

> o Funded in collaboration with HEIs to promote agripreneurship and self-employment.

• Skill Development and Livelihood Projects:

> o Training programs on organic farming, dairy, food processing, and value addition.

• Student Exposure Visits and Internships:

> o Field immersion to understand rural ecosystems and policy implementation.

• Support for Technology Transfer:

> o Facilitate adoption of HEI-developed technologies in rural sectors (e.g., irrigation tools, agri-machinery).

**218.3. Eligible Institutions**

• Agricultural universities, rural institutes, and HEIs with:

> o Departments of agriculture, rural development, economics, or environmental sciences.

• Colleges with active Extension Education Units, KVKs, or incubation centres.

**218.4. NABARD-Supported Initiatives**

• Rural Innovation Fund (RIF):

> o Funding support for innovative, low-cost rural solutions developed in HEIs.

• Farm Sector Promotion Fund (FSPF) and Watershed Development Projects:

> o Collaboration with HEIs for research, evaluation, and technical backstopping.

• Climate Resilient Agriculture and Tribal Development Programs:

> o Involvement of HEIs for research support and impact monitoring.

• Financial Literacy and Inclusion Campaigns:

> o Training of students to conduct outreach in rural and tribal areas.

**218.5. Benefits to Students and Faculty**

• Opportunity to work on real-world, impact-driven rural projects.

• Access to research grants, field exposure, and live data.

• Capacity to contribute to policy research, evaluation studies, and innovation trials.

• Increased employability in rural banking, NGOs, CSR roles, and development sector.

**218.6. Institutional Advantages**

• Recognition as a rural innovation and development hub.

• Enhanced performance in NAAC/NIRF and societal impact rankings.

• Establishment of NABARD Chairs/Research Units for long-term collaboration.

• Scope for community engagement, interdisciplinary projects, and rural incubators.

**218.7. How to Collaborate with NABARD**

• Submit research/extension project proposals aligned with NABARD’s priority sectors.

• Apply for recognition under NABARD’s capacity building or development support schemes.

• Build MoUs between HEI and NABARD regional offices.

• Join as a knowledge partner in NABARD-sponsored evaluation or pilot projects

**219. Startup India Initiatives in Higher Education Institutions**

**219.1. Objectives of Startup India in HEIs**

• Foster a culture of innovation, problem-solving, and entrepreneurship among students and faculty.

• Enable HEIs to become launchpads for student-led start-ups.

• Create a supportive ecosystem through incubation, mentoring, and funding.

• Align academic activities with national innovation and start-up policies.

**219.2. Key Startup India Programs for HEIs**

• National Innovation and Startup Policy (NISP) 2019:

> o Guideline framework for HEIs to integrate entrepreneurship in curriculum, governance, and funding.

• Institution Innovation Councils (IICs) (by MHRD/AICTE & MoE’s Innovation Cell):

> o Formed in colleges to promote innovation activities and start-up awareness.

• Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS):

> o Provides financial assistance to start-ups through HEI-based incubators.

• Smart India Hackathon / Toycathon:

> o National-level problem-solving events encouraging start-up creation from student ideas.

• Startup India Yatra:

> o Outreach program that visits campuses to conduct bootcamps, pitch sessions, and mentor talks.

**219.3. Role of HEIs in Startup India Ecosystem**

• Establish and manage Incubation Centres or Entrepreneurship Development Cells (EDCs).

• Integrate startup-related courses, electives, and credit systems into curriculum.

• Offer pre-incubation support, including idea validation, team formation, and prototype development.

• Facilitate industry-academia linkage for market access and co-innovation.

**219.4. Support Available to HEIs**

• Recognition as Host Institutions (HI) for seed funding or TBI support.

• Access to Startup India portal and dashboard for networking, mentorship, and funding.

• Eligibility for central schemes like:

> o NIDHI-TBI (by DST)
>
> o MSME incubation funding
>
> o AICTE SPICES, ARIIA ranking incentives

• Collaboration with state start-up missions and accelerators.

**219.5. Benefits to Students and Faculty**

• Opportunity to launch and scale start-ups from campus.

• Access to incubation, mentoring, IP support, and government funding.

• Recognition through national awards, grants, and investor connections.

• Improved career pathways through start-up leadership or co-founding roles.

**219.6. Impact Metrics and Outcomes**

• No. of start-ups incubated and commercialized.

• Patents filed, products launched, and jobs created.

• Student participation in hackathons, idea contests, and start-up bootcamps.

• Institutional ranking and branding through ARIIA and NISP adoption.

**219.7. Implementation Roadmap for HEIs**

• Form a Startup/Innovation Committee with faculty and industry experts.

• Register for Institution’s Innovation Council (IIC) via MIC portal.

• Create a Start-up Policy and Strategic Plan aligned with NISP 2019.

• Launch an on-campus incubator or co-working space.

• Facilitate regular events, competitions, and investor networking.

**220. SIDBI (Small Industries Development Bank of India) in Higher Education Institutions**

**220.1. Objectives of SIDBI Involvement in HEIs**

• Promote entrepreneurship development and financing awareness among students and faculty.

• Facilitate start-up incubation, MSME support, and financial literacy through academic collaboration.

• Bridge the gap between academic innovation and commercial enterprise.

• Support HEIs in building a sustainable start-up ecosystem.

**220.2. Key SIDBI Programs Relevant to HEIs**

• SIDBI Vision 2.0:

> o Focuses on collaboration with Incubators in HEIs to promote early-stage ventures.

• Funds of Funds for Startups (FFS):

> o SIDBI manages FFS under Startup India, where start-ups incubated in HEIs can indirectly benefit through venture funds.

• Udyam Abhilasha Program:

> o Conducted in colleges to train students in entrepreneurship and MSME development.

• SIDBI-Supported Incubators and Start-up Funds:

> o Partner with TBIs in HEIs to mentor and invest in innovative student start-ups.

**220.3. Role of HEIs in SIDBI Ecosystem**

• Establish Incubation/Innovation Centres eligible for SIDBI collaboration.

• Host entrepreneurship awareness camps and training programs funded by SIDBI.

• Identify and handhold potential MSMEs and start-ups for seed funding and credit linkage.

• Facilitate student business plans to get validated and connected to SIDBI's network.

**220.4. Support Provided by SIDBI**

• Seed capital support for early-stage start-ups via partner incubators.

• Mentorship, credit facilitation, and access to MSME finance tools.

• Funding for entrepreneurship training workshops and exposure visits.

• Access to SIDBI’s e-platforms such as:

> o Stand-Up Mitra
>
> o Udyamimitra Portal
>
> o www.indsamachar.in for MSME news and schemes

**220.5. Benefits to Students and Faculty**

• Opportunity to launch ventures with financial backing from SIDBI-linked funds.

• Gain exposure to MSME policy, finance, and operational models.

• Access to credit-readiness bootcamps, mentoring, and investor connect programs.

• Encouragement to convert final-year projects and innovations into viable start-ups.

**220.6. Institutional Benefits**

• Recognition as SIDBI partner incubators or entrepreneurship hubs.

• Improved performance in ARIIA, NISP, and NAAC innovation metrics.

• Eligibility for funding, capacity building, and start-up accelerator programs.

• Opportunities for long-term partnerships in MSME promotion.

**220.7. Suggested Action Plan for HEIs**

• Set up an Entrepreneurship Development Cell (EDC) or TBI.

• Reach out to SIDBI for:

> o Partnership proposals
>
> o Workshop grants
>
> o Startup/idea contests sponsorship

• Encourage student teams to prepare bankable business plans for funding linkage.

• Organize SIDBI-led credit clinics, MSME finance awareness, and startup pitching events.

**221. NSIC (National Small Industries Corporation) in Higher Education Institutions**

**221.1. Objectives of NSIC Involvement in HEIs**

• Promote entrepreneurial skills and MSME development among students and faculty.

• Enable academic institutions to support small-scale industries through skill-based training.

• Foster industry-institute interaction by bridging the gap between education and entrepreneurship.

• Support start-up creation, technology transfer, and business incubation in HEIs.

**221.2. Key NSIC Programs Relevant to HEIs**

• NSIC-Technical Services Centres (NTSCs):

> o Provides technical training, skill development, and incubation support.

• NSIC Rapid Incubation Programme (RIP):

> o Aims to incubate early-stage entrepreneurs, especially students, with modular infrastructure and training.

• Entrepreneurship Skill Development Programs (ESDPs):

> o Conducted in colleges for promoting self-employment and small business setups.

• Technical and Management Training Courses:

> o Tailored short-term and long-term skill enhancement programs in collaboration with HEIs.

**221.3. Role of HEIs in NSIC Ecosystem**

• Host institution for NSIC incubation centres or training programs.

• Partner in conducting ESDPs, awareness camps, and industrial visits.

• Facilitate student and faculty projects that align with MSME innovation needs.

• Encourage industry collaboration using NSIC's vendor development and marketing platforms.

**221.4. Support Provided by NSIC to HEIs**

• Setup of incubation centres with machinery, tools, and training modules.

• Access to NTSC labs and facilities for hands-on training.

• Guidance on project report preparation, MSME registration, and business setup.

• Market support schemes like e-Marketing, Government e-Marketplace (GeM), and credit facilitation.

**221.5. Benefits to Students and Faculty**

• Learn practical skills aligned with MSME sector needs.

• Get training in business model design, cost estimation, and quality control.

• Access to NSIC's mentorship and project implementation network.

• Launch student ventures through NSIC-assisted incubation and market linkage.

**221.6. Institutional Benefits**

• Recognition as a Centre for MSME Excellence or Entrepreneurship Hub.

• Access to government schemes, funding, and industry connections.

• Improved performance in NAAC, NIRF, and ARIIA rankings through innovation and outreach.

• Opportunity to integrate vocational education and skill-based courses into the curriculum.

**221.7. Suggested Action Plan for HEIs**

• Sign an MoU with NSIC for incubation or training centre setup.

• Launch entrepreneurship awareness drives and Rapid Incubation Programs (RIPs).

• Encourage students to participate in NSIC live projects, exhibitions, and product development.

• Leverage NSIC expertise to support rural entrepreneurship and local industry engagement.

**222. Proposal Format for Establishing a Rapid Incubation Centre (RIC) in a Higher Education Institution (HEI), aligned with NSIC guidelines**

**222.1. Cover Page**

• Title: Proposal for Establishment of Rapid Incubation Centre (RIC)

• Name of Institution

• Address with Contact Details

• Submitted to: National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC)

• Date of Submission

**222.2. Executive Summary**

• Brief overview of the institution

• Objective of establishing the RIC

• Summary of proposed infrastructure, focus sectors, and expected outcomes

**222.3. Institutional Profile**

• Name, type (University/College/Technical Institute), and year of establishment

• Approvals and accreditations (AICTE/UGC/NAAC/NBA)

• Existing departments relevant to entrepreneurship, innovation, or MSMEs

• Details of existing incubation/entrepreneurship/skill development activities

**222.4. Vision and Objectives of the Proposed RIC**

• Promote entrepreneurship and MSME development among students

• Support skill-based incubation and product-based training

• Foster innovation in priority sectors (agri-tech, food processing, handicrafts, etc.)

• Build local employment and enterprise capacity

**222.5. Proposed Infrastructure and Resources**

• Space Allocation: Rooms/workshops/labs (in sq. ft.)

• Facilities Available: Internet, power backup, tools and equipment (if any)

• Staffing Plan: Incubation coordinator, trainers, support staff

**222.6. Training and Incubation Plan**

• Proposed Duration of training programs (3–6 months)

• Skill Areas covered (e.g., food processing, electronics assembly, handicraft tools)

• Batch Size and Frequency

• Curriculum outline: technical, financial, marketing, and soft skills

**222.7. Target Beneficiaries**

• Final year students, unemployed youth, early-stage entrepreneurs

• Focus on SC/ST/OBC/women entrepreneurs (if applicable)

• Estimated number of trainees per year

**222.8. Financial Requirements**

• Capital Expenses (CAPEX):

> o Machinery, tools, furniture, training kits

• Recurring Expenses (OPEX):

> o Trainer salary, consumables, marketing, maintenance

• Funding Request from NSIC (with justification)

• Institutional Contribution (space, manpower, utilities)

**222.9. Sustainability and Revenue Plan**

• Nominal fee collection from trainees

• Commercialization of student innovations

• Consultancy, sponsored workshops, or product sales

**222.10. Expected Outcomes and Impact**

• No. of trainees incubated annually

• Start-ups/MSMEs created

• Local employment generated

• Contributions to the regional entrepreneurial ecosystem

**222.11. Monitoring and Evaluation**

• KPIs for success (start-up creation, placement, skill certification)

• Internal evaluation and third-party assessments

• Reporting mechanism to NSIC

**222.12. Annexures**

• Letter of Intent from Institution Head

• Building layout or photos of proposed space

• Faculty CVs

• Budget estimates with vendor quotations

• MoUs with MSMEs or industry partners (if any)

• Previous EDC/Startup/Incubation activities (photos/events/publications)

**223. Government Schemes and Start-up Grants for Campus Incubators in HEIs**

**223.1. Central Government Schemes**

1\. Startup India Seed Fund Scheme (SISFS) – DPIIT

• Supports: Campus incubators to fund student and early-stage start-ups.

• Components:

> o ₹20 lakhs for idea validation (PoC)
>
> o ₹50 lakhs for product development and market entry

• Eligibility: DPIIT-recognised incubators

• Website: seedfund.startupindia.gov.in

2\. NIDHI – PRAYAS (DST)

• **Supports:** HEIs to establish PRAYAS Centres for prototype development

• **Funding:** Up to ₹10 lakhs per innovator

• **Focus:** Hardware-based innovations

• **Eligibility:** DST-approved Technology Business Incubators (TBIs)

• **Website:** nidhi-dst.org

3\. NIDHI – EIR (Entrepreneur-in-Residence)

• **Supports:** Campus start-up fellows with a monthly stipend

• **Funding:** ₹30,000–₹50,000/month for 12 months

• **Target:** Student entrepreneurs working on high-risk ideas

4\. MSME Innovative Scheme

• Supports: Incubators in HEIs for technology development and MSME linkage

• Funding:

> o ₹15 lakhs per idea (student/faculty start-ups)
>
> o Up to ₹1 crore for commercialization

• Eligibility: Incubator must be registered with Ministry of MSME

• Website: https://innovative.msme.gov.in

5\. *TIDE 2.0 – MeitY*

• Supports: Technology incubators focused on ICT, AI, IoT, robotics

• Funding:

> o Idea-stage: ₹4 lakhs
>
> o Start-up stage: ₹7 lakhs

• Eligibility: HEIs with an existing incubation centre in digital tech

6\. Atal Incubation Centres (AIC) – NITI Aayog (AIM)

• **Funding:** Up to ₹10 crore over 5 years

• **Objective:** Support sector-specific incubators in HEIs

• **Eligibility:** Public/private HEIs with innovation track record

• **Website:** aim.gov.in

7\. *BioNEST – DBT BIRAC*

• **Supports:** Biotechnology incubators in HEIs and R&D institutions

• Funding: Infrastructure + operational support

• **Focus:** Life sciences, healthcare, agri-bio, and industrial biotech

• **Website:** birac.nic.in

**223.2. State Government Schemes (Examples)**

• Tamil Nadu Startup and Innovation Mission (TANSIM)

• Kerala Startup Mission (KSUM)

• Maharashtra State Innovation Society (MSINS)

• Startup Odisha, Startup Karnataka, Startup Punjab etc.

• Most provide:

> o Seed funding (₹5–25 lakhs)
>
> o Mentorship and incubation support
>
> o Reimbursements for patent, marketing, and infrastructure

**223.3. Other Supportive Government Programs**

• SIDBI Fund of Funds for Startups (FFS) – venture capital route for HEI start-ups

• Stand-Up India Scheme – for women and SC/ST founders

• PM YUVA Yojana (Education Ministry) – entrepreneurship education support in HEIs

• AICTE SPICES/IDEA Lab – support for institutional innovation ecosystems

• NSIC Rapid Incubation Program – support for skill-based campus incubation

**224. Industry-Sponsored Research in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)**

**224.1. Objectives of Industry-Sponsored Research in HEIs**

• Leverage academic expertise to solve real-world industrial problems.

• Foster collaborative R&D leading to commercial applications.

• Enhance innovation and product development capacity in both academia and industry.

• Provide students and faculty with hands-on experience in industry-relevant projects.

**224.2. Key Features**

• Funded directly by private sector companies or industry associations.

• Focus on applied research, prototype development, process optimization, and market innovation.

• Involves joint supervision, IP co-ownership, and often non-disclosure agreements (NDAs).

• May include internships, sabbaticals, or joint labs set up on campus.

**224.3. Common Industry Partners**

• **Tech companies:** Google, IBM, Microsoft, Infosys

• **Automotive:** Tata Motors, Mahindra, Bosch

• **Pharma & Biotech:** Dr. Reddy's, Cipla, Biocon

• **FMCG & Agri:** ITC, Godrej Agrovet

• **Startups and MSMEs:** Via incubator-linked collaborations

**224.4. Types of Sponsored Research Activities**

• Product/Process Development

• Design and Testing Services

• Market and User Research

• Sustainability and Energy Audits

• AI/ML, IoT, and Automation Solutions

• Material Innovation and Simulation Studies

**224.5. Benefits to HEIs**

• Access to funding, industrial equipment, and real-time data.

• Improved placement opportunities and internships for students.

• Strengthening of curriculum through practical exposure.

• Enhanced chances of patents, consultancy income, and spin-off companies.

**224.6. Benefits to Industry**

• Cost-effective outsourcing of R&D tasks.

• Access to faculty expertise and student innovation.

• Opportunity to co-develop IP and explore new markets.

• Enhanced CSR impact and brand presence in academia.

**224.7. Funding and Support**

• Funding ranges: ₹5 lakhs to ₹5 crores+, depending on scope.

• Components supported:

> o Manpower (JRF/SRF)
>
> o Equipment and software
>
> o Prototyping, field trials, and testing
>
> o Conferences, reports, and publications

**224.8. How to Initiate Industry-Sponsored Research**

• Set up a Corporate Relations Cell or Industry Liaison Office in HEI.

• Identify mutual interests and map them to academic strengths.

• Sign MoUs or NDAs for confidentiality and collaboration terms.

• Prepare joint proposals with defined deliverables, milestones, and IP sharing.

**224.9. Challenges and Solutions**

• IP ownership disputes:

> o Solution: Use clear IP and royalty-sharing agreements.

• Mismatch in timelines and expectations:

> o Solution: Set realistic goals and project management plans.

• Low industry trust in academia:

> o Solution: Start with pilot collaborations and showcase successful case studies.

**224.10. Examples of Best Practices**

• IITs and NITs partnering with global corporations for innovation labs.

• Private universities running joint certificate programs and research hubs.

• Hackathons and Innovation Challenges run by companies to seed research ideas.

**226. National Education Policy (NEP) and Financing of Education and Research in Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)**

**226.1. NEP 2020: Vision for Financing Education and Research**

• NEP 2020 emphasizes significantly increasing public investment in education to reach 6% of GDP.

• Aims to revamp research infrastructure and ensure equitable funding across HEIs, disciplines, and regions.

• Calls for establishing the National Research Foundation (NRF) to provide merit-based and peer-reviewed research funding.

**226.2. Key NEP Recommendations on Research Funding**

• Establishment of NRF:

> o Central agency to fund research across science, technology, humanities, and social sciences.
>
> o Focus on building research capacity in public and private HEIs, especially state universities.

• Increase institutional autonomy in managing research funds.

• Encourage interdisciplinary and mission-driven research aligned with national development goals.

**226.3. Sources of Research Financing for HEIs**

• Government Budget Allocation:

> o UGC, AICTE, DST, DBT, ICSSR, ICMR, DRDO, ICAR, and MoE schemes.

• National Research Foundation (NRF) (proposed):

> o ₹50,000 crore over 5 years to fund HEI-based research and innovation.

• State Government Support:

> o Funds for state universities through RUSA and state-level innovation missions.

• Industry and CSR:

> o Industry-sponsored research projects and CSR-funded innovation labs.

• International Agencies:

> o World Bank, UNDP, EU Horizon, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, etc.

• Alumni Contributions and Philanthropy:

> o Endowment funds, research chairs, and sponsored labs.

**226.4. NEP's Focus Areas for Research Investment**

• **STEM and Emerging Technologies:** AI, robotics, data science, quantum computing.

• **Social Sciences and Policy Research:** Education, governance, environment, gender studies.

• **Rural and Community-Based Research:** Agri-tech, water, sanitation, rural entrepreneurship.

• **Undergraduate Research:** Promoting inquiry-based learning in UG programs.

**226.5. Financial Reforms Proposed under NEP**

• Greater autonomy to HEIs in budget allocation and research administration.

• Development of Institutional Development Plans (IDPs) to align funding with academic goals.

• Outcome-based funding linked to research impact and institutional performance.

• Creation of HECI (Higher Education Commission of India) with financial regulatory functions under HEFA (Higher Education Financing Agency).

**226.6. Challenges in Financing Research in HEIs**

• Disparity in fund distribution between elite and regional institutions.

• Delayed disbursal and administrative bottlenecks.

• Lack of professional grant writing and fund utilization training.

• Limited collaboration between academia and industry.

**226.7. Solutions and Opportunities**

• Establish Research and Innovation Cells (RICs) in all HEIs.

• Train faculty and administrators in project writing, grant management, and financial compliance.

• Create joint research consortiums between central, state, and private HEIs.

• Promote public-private research funding models.

**227. National Research Foundation (NRF)**

**227.1. Introduction to NRF**

• Full Name: National Research Foundation

• Proposed under the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020.

• Aims to strengthen research culture across disciplines in India.

• Will act as an umbrella body to fund, coordinate, and promote high-quality research across HEIs, national labs, and industry.

**227.2. Objectives of NRF**

• Promote interdisciplinary, high-impact research across science, technology, social sciences, and humanities.

• Support cutting-edge innovation and bridge gaps between academia and industry.

• Provide equitable funding to state universities, private HEIs, and research institutes.

• Encourage undergraduate research, especially in Tier II and III institutions.

• Build research infrastructure and foster a culture of inquiry and problem-solving.

**227.3. Key Functions**

• Disburse research grants and fellowships at scale across domains.

• Establish thematic research missions and national grand challenges.

• Evaluate and monitor project performance and impact.

• Partner with:

> o Government research agencies (DST, DBT, ICMR, CSIR)
>
> o Industry bodies and international research organizations

• Serve as a central funding agency similar to NSF (USA) or UKRI (UK).

**227.4. Structure of NRF**

• Governing Board chaired by the Prime Minister of India.

• Executive Council headed by eminent scientists, technologists, and educationists.

• Four Major Divisions:

> o Sciences
>
> o Technology
>
> o Social Sciences and Arts
>
> o Strategic Areas (including defense, energy, and environment)

**227.5. Funding Strategy**

• Estimated Budget: ₹50,000 crores over 5 years (as per NEP 2020)

• Sources:

> o Government grants
>
> o Private industry partnerships
>
> o International agencies and philanthropic contributions

• Allocation Mechanism:

> o Based on peer review
>
> o Focus on outcomes, innovation, and societal relevance

**227.6. Benefits for HEIs**

• Access to competitive research funding, especially for non-IIT/IISc institutions.

• Support to build research labs, recruit staff, and upgrade infrastructure.

• Opportunities for collaborative research with national and international institutions.

• Encourages faculty-student research engagement from UG to PhD level.

• Improved global visibility, publications, and patents.

**227.7. Expected Impact**

• Democratization of research by funding State and Private HEIs.

• Promotion of research-based learning in undergraduate education.

• Boost India's global R&D rankings and innovation output.

• Strengthen evidence-based policy making through social science and humanities research.

• Foster cross-disciplinary solutions for national and global challenges.

**228. Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) in Higher Education Institutions**

**228.1. Role of MoEFCC in HEIs**

• Promote environmental education, awareness, and research in academic institutions.

• Support capacity building and innovation in climate action, biodiversity, and sustainability.

• Collaborate with HEIs to develop climate-resilient technologies and green solutions.

• Encourage student and faculty engagement in national environmental initiatives.

**228.2. Key MoEFCC-Supported Programs in HEIs**

**A. National Green Corps (Eco Clubs)**

• Active in schools and colleges to promote eco-literacy and student-led environmental action.

• Activities: clean-up drives, tree plantation, waste management campaigns.

**B. Environmental Information System (ENVIS)**

• ENVIS Centres in selected HEIs for data collection, awareness, and research dissemination.

• Focus areas: forestry, climate change, pollution, wetlands, etc.

**C. National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC)**

• HEIs participate as knowledge partners in research and monitoring of climate adaptation projects.

**D. Green Skill Development Programme (GSDP)**

• Provides certification-based training programs in environmental and forest-related skills.

• Targeted at students, researchers, and unemployed youth in HEIs.

**E. National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC)**

• Research partnerships with HEIs under missions like:

> o National Solar Mission
>
> o National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture
>
> o National Water Mission

**228.3. Research & Project Funding Opportunities**

• Sponsorship of Environment Impact Assessment (EIA), forest restoration, biodiversity surveys.

• Funding for pilot studies and technology demonstrations on waste, water, and energy.

• Support for:

> o Faculty-led projects on environmental modeling and policy research.
>
> o Student dissertations and PhDs in environmental sciences.

• MoEFCC Fellowship schemes for M.Sc./PhD candidates in ecology, wildlife, and climate policy.

**228.4. Institutional Benefits**

• Recognition as MoEFCC knowledge partners or regional centres of excellence.

• Eligibility to host:

> o ENVIS centres, GSDP training hubs, or research field stations.

• Boosts performance in NAAC/NIRF rankings under environmental criteria.

• Facilitates international collaborations in environment and climate research.

**228.5. Recommended Activities for HEIs**

• Integrate environmental science and sustainability into UG/PG curriculum.

• Host Green Campus Initiatives (solar power, water conservation, zero-waste campus).

• Conduct MoEFCC-funded workshops, awareness drives, and research symposiums.

• Encourage interdisciplinary climate research in collaboration with ministries and NGOs.

**229. MoEFCC-Funded Research Schemes for Higher Education Institutions (HEIs)**

**229.1. Environmental Information System (ENVIS) Scheme**

• Objective: Support HEIs in establishing ENVIS Resource Partner Centres.

• Focus Areas: Biodiversity, forests, pollution control, eco-tourism, wetlands, climate change.

• Support:

> o Infrastructure for data collection & dissemination.
>
> o Outreach & publication activities.

• Eligible Institutions: HEIs with relevant departments (e.g., Environmental Science, Botany, Forestry).

• More Info: http://www.envis.nic.in

**229.2. National Mission on Himalayan Studies (NMHS)**

• Objective: Promote research and innovation in the Indian Himalayan Region.

• Focus Areas: Ecosystem services, sustainable agriculture, water resources, climate resilience.

• Funding:

> o Thematic research grants for HEIs in or working on Himalayan states.
>
> o Fellowships for PhD and postdocs.

• More Info: http://nmhs.org.in

**229.3. National Adaptation Fund for Climate Change (NAFCC) – R&D Component**

• Objective: Conduct climate change adaptation studies and impact analysis.

• HEI Role:

> o Knowledge partners for state projects.
>
> o Monitoring & Evaluation support.

• Eligible Projects: Climate-resilient agriculture, water conservation, forest restoration.

**229.4. Green Skill Development Programme (GSDP)**

• Objective: Build employable green skills in youth through HEIs.

• Focus Areas:

> o Wildlife management, waste management, ecotourism, pollution monitoring.

• HEI Role:

> o Host GSDP training centres.
>
> o Offer MoEFCC-certified short-term courses.

• Funding Includes:

> o Training materials, expert honorariums, student kits, certification.

**229.5. Research and Development in Environment Sector (RDES)**

• Objective: Provide grant-in-aid to HEIs for environment-related research.

• Key Themes:

> o E-waste, air/water pollution, environmental governance, green infrastructure.

• Funding:

> o ₹20–75 lakhs per project depending on scale and duration (typically 2–3 years).

• Application:

> o Call for proposals issued on MoEFCC or R&D division website.

• More Info: Often published via https://moef.gov.in/

**229.6. National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC) – Mission-Based Research**

• HEIs can contribute under missions like:

> o National Water Mission
>
> o National Solar Mission
>
> o National Mission for Sustainable Agriculture

• MoEFCC role: Funding thematic research aligned with NAPCC goals.

**229.7. National Biodiversity Action Plan (NBAP) – Institutional Research Support**

• Objective: Promote conservation science and biodiversity planning in HEIs.

• Scope:

> o Species documentation
>
> o GIS mapping
>
> o Traditional knowledge systems

• Often partnered with: National Biodiversity Authority (NBA), State Biodiversity Boards.

**230. SAMPLE RESEARCH STRATEGY PLAN**

Aligned with NEP 2020 Goals

\[Institution Name\] \| Timeframe: 2025–2030

**1. Vision Statement**

To cultivate a robust and inclusive research ecosystem that fosters interdisciplinary, impactful, and socially relevant research, aligned with the vision of NEP 2020 and national development priorities.

**2. Strategic Objectives**

• Promote a culture of inquiry and innovation across all disciplines.

• Build and support world-class research infrastructure and human capital.

• Align research with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and national missions.

• Facilitate industry-academia collaborations and technology commercialization.

• Strengthen data-driven and evidence-based policymaking through social science research.

**230.3. Institutional Priorities (5-Year Goals)**

| **Priority Area**              | **Goal**                                                             |
|--------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Interdisciplinary Research** | Establish 3 research clusters (e.g., Health + AI, Agriculture + IoT) |
| **Research at UG Level**       | 30% of UG students engaged in research projects by 2030              |
| **External Funding**           | Increase sponsored research by 50%                                   |
| **Research Capacity**          | Train 100 faculty in research methodology & grant writing            |
| **Innovation Output**          | File 25 patents and incubate 10 start-ups                            |

NEP Alignment:

• Multidisciplinary approach

• UG research integration

• Funding diversification

• Faculty development

• Innovation & incubation

**230.4. Structural Framework**

• **Research & Development Cell (RDC):** Central body for research planning and implementation

• **Thematic Research Groups (TRGs):** Cross-departmental teams based on societal challenges

• **Research Advisory Board:** Faculty + industry + alumni experts to guide research directions

• **Research Support Office (RSO):** Proposal drafting, grant management, ethics clearance

**230.5. Key Focus Areas**

• **STEM Research:** Clean energy, AI, advanced materials, biotechnology

• **Social Sciences & Policy:** Education reform, urban development, public health

• **Humanities:** Indian knowledge systems, linguistics, digital archives

• **Sustainability:** Climate resilience, water resources, rural innovation

**230.6. Research Funding Strategy**

• Tap into:

> o National: NRF, DST, DBT, ICSSR, MoE, MSME
>
> o International: EU Horizon, British Council, DAAD
>
> o Industry: CSR collaborations, R&D sponsorships

• Create Internal Research Seed Grant (IRSG) for early-stage faculty proposals

• Incentivize funded research with recognition and workload reduction

**230.7. Undergraduate and Postgraduate Research Integration**

• Introduce research methodology modules from UG second year

• Launch Student Research Fellowships (SRF-U)

• Host annual Student Research Symposium and innovation contests

• Mandatory research component in all PG programs

**230.8. Research Capacity Building**

• Conduct regular:

> o FDPs on proposal writing, data analysis, and ethics
>
> o Workshops on IP, patenting, and publishing

• Partner with external bodies for faculty research exchange and sabbaticals

**230.9. Knowledge Dissemination**

• Establish Open Access Institutional Repository

• Launch peer-reviewed institutional journals

• Host National/International Conferences on priority themes

• Support multi-language and local research translation

**230.10. Monitoring and Evaluation**

| **Metric**                           | **Target**                  |
|--------------------------------------|-----------------------------|
| **Research Publications**            | Increase by 100% in 5 years |
| **External Grants Secured**          | ₹10 crore by 2030           |
| **No. of Student Research Projects** | 300+ annually               |
| **Industry-funded Projects**         | 15 by 2030                  |
| **No. of IPs Filed**                 | 5 per year                  |

**230.11. Sustainability and NEP Linkage**

Aligns with NEP goals of:

> o Creating a vibrant research ecosystem
>
> o Bringing research to all levels of education
>
> o Equitable access to funding and infrastructure

Built-in mechanisms for:

> o Inclusivity
>
> o Local problem solving
>
> o Global collaboration
